facts.fact: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I.
Saint Vidyaranya is credited with inspiring the founding of Vijayanagara.
Tradition names five Sangama brothers — Harihara, Bukka, Kampana, Mudappa and Marappa — named after their father Sangama.
The capital Vijayanagara (Hampi) stood on the Tungabhadra.
Hampi is named after the local goddess Pampadevi.
By 1346 the Hoysala kingdom had passed to Vijayanagara.
Vijayanagara was also called the Karnataka kingdom.
The empire stretched from the river Krishna in the north to the far south of the peninsula.
Four dynasties ruled Vijayanagara in order: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu.
Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) belonged to the Tuluva dynasty.
Babur's Baburnama called Krishnadevaraya the most powerful ruler of India.
Krishnadevaraya was titled 'Andhra Bhoja'.
Krishnadevaraya wrote Amuktamalyada, a Telugu work on polity.
Krishnadevaraya wrote Jambavati Kalyanam in Sanskrit.
The Ashtadiggajas were the eight great Telugu poets of Krishnadevaraya's court.
Krishnadevaraya is credited (UPSC 2020 key) with a large dam and canal-cum-aqueduct across the Tungabhadra.
The Raichur Doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra was the core of the Vijayanagara–Bahmani rivalry.
Domingo Paes was a Portuguese traveller.
Nicolo de Conti was an Italian traveller.
Abdur Razzaq was a Persian ambassador.
Fernao Nunes was a Portuguese historian (chronicler).
Vijayanagara administrative units from largest to smallest: Mandala, Nadu, Sthala, Grama.
The Vittala temple at Hampi is famous for its musical pillars and stone chariot.
Vijayanagara temple architecture belongs to the Dravidian tradition.
Carnatic music and Kuchipudi flourished under Vijayanagara.
Yakshaganam theatre flourished in the Vijayanagara period.
The Battle of Talikota was fought in 1565.
Vijayanagara was led at Talikota by Aliya Rama Raya.
The Talikota coalition was Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar and Bidar.
After Talikota Hampi was looted and abandoned.
War-horse trade via the Portuguese fuelled the Vijayanagara–Bahmani rivalry.
The Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347 by Alauddin Bahman Shah.
Alauddin Bahman Shah was also known as Hasan Gangu.
The Bahmani kingdom began by declaring independence from the Delhi Sultanate.
Ahmad Shah Wali shifted the Bahmani capital from Gulbarga to Bidar.
Firoz Shah Bahmani built an observatory near Daulatabad.
Mahmud Gawan, an Iranian trader, rose to be Prime Minister of the Bahmani kingdom.
Mahmud Gawan built a three-storeyed madrasa at Bidar.
Mahmud Gawan was executed in 1481.
The Bahmani kingdom was divided into eight provinces called tarafs, each under a Tarafdar.
Bahmani nobles were split between Deccanis (locals) and Afaqis or Pardesis (newcomers).
The Bahmani army used gunpowder.
The Bahmani kingdom broke into Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmednagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutub Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi) and Bidar (Barid Shahi).
The Charminar at Hyderabad was built by Muhammad Quli Qutub Shah.
Gesu Daraz of Gulbarga wrote in Dakhini Urdu, which became prominent under the Bahmanis.
Mahmud Gawan wrote the Riyaz-ul-Insha.
Bahmani nobles were paid in cash or jagirs.
Ayagars were the hereditary village officers of Vijayanagara.
The early Sangama seat was Anegondi, on the north bank of the Tungabhadra, before the capital moved across the river to Vijayanagara (Hampi).
Harihara I, the founder, ruled 1336–1356.
Bukka Raya I (1356–1377) sent an embassy to the Ming emperor of China (1374).
Kumara Kampana, son of Bukka I, destroyed the Madurai Sultanate (c.1371).
Gangadevi, wife of Kumara Kampana, described his conquest of Madurai in the Sanskrit poem Madhuravijayam.
Harihara II (1377–1404) was the first Sangama king to take imperial titles such as Maharajadhiraja.
Sayana, brother of Vidyaranya (Madhava), wrote the Vedarthaprakasha commentary on the Vedas under Bukka I and Harihara II.
Vidyaranya is credited with the Rajakalanirnaya.
Fernao Nunes credits Deva Raya I (1406–1422) with a dam across the Tungabhadra (c.1410) and a channel into the city.
Deva Raya I defeated Firoz Shah Bahmani at Pangal in 1420.
The Italian Nicolo de Conti visited Vijayanagara in 1420, in the reign of Deva Raya I.
Deva Raya II (1424–1446), the greatest Sangama king, recruited Muslim (Turkish) archers into his army.
Deva Raya II took the title 'Gajabetekara' (hunter of elephants).
Abdur Razzaq, envoy of the Timurid Shah Rukh, visited Vijayanagara in 1443 under Deva Raya II.
Kumaravyasa wrote the Kannada Mahabharata (Karnata Bharata Kathamanjari) in Deva Raya II's time.
The Telugu poet Srinatha was honoured with a kanakabhishekam (bath of gold coins) at Deva Raya II's court.
Mallikarjuna Raya (1446–1465) and Virupaksha Raya II (1465–1485) were weak kings; Praudha Raya (1485) was the last Sangama.
Saluva Narasimha (1485–1491), governor of Chandragiri, seized the throne from the Sangamas — the first usurpation.
Tallapaka Annamacharya, composer of Telugu sankirtanas to Venkateswara of Tirumala, was patronised by Saluva Narasimha.
Tuluva Narasa Nayaka was regent and real ruler under Narasimha Raya II (Immadi Narasimha).
Vira Narasimha, son of Narasa Nayaka, deposed Narasimha Raya II in 1505 (the second usurpation) and began the Tuluva dynasty.
Krishnadevaraya captured Udayagiri (1514) from the Gajapatis of Odisha.
Krishnadevaraya took Kondavidu (1515) from the Gajapati king Prataparudra.
After the Kalinga campaign Krishnadevaraya set up a victory pillar at Potnuru near Simhachalam.
Krishnadevaraya defeated Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur at the Battle of Raichur in 1520.
Krishnadevaraya restored the Bahmani sultan Mahmud Shah and took the title 'Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya'.
Krishnadevaraya was also called 'Mooru Rayara Ganda' (king of three kings) and 'Kannada Rajya Rama Ramana'.
Krishnadevaraya built Nagalapura (modern Hospet) in memory of his mother Nagala Devi.
Krishnadevaraya built the Krishna temple at Hampi (1513) for a Bala Krishna image brought from Udayagiri.
Amuktamalyada tells the story of Andal (Goda) and Periyalvar and was composed after a dream of Andhra Vishnu at Srikakulam (Krishna district).
The line 'Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa' (Telugu is the finest of the land's languages) is from Amuktamalyada.
Copper statues of Krishnadevaraya with his queens Chinna Devi and Tirumala Devi stand at the Tirumala temple.
Purandaradasa, honoured as the Pitamaha (father) of Carnatic music, lived in the age of Krishnadevaraya.
The Portuguese Duarte Barbosa (c.1516) praised the religious tolerance of Vijayanagara.
Domingo Paes visited Vijayanagara c.1520–22, in the reign of Krishnadevaraya.
Allasani Peddana, the Andhra Kavita Pitamaha, wrote the Manucharitramu (Svarochisha Manusambhavamu).
Nandi Thimmana (Mukku Thimmana) wrote the Parijatapaharanamu.
Dhurjati wrote the Sri Kalahastiswara Mahatmyamu and the Kalahastiswara Satakam.
Madayyagari Mallana wrote the Rajasekhara Charitramu.
Ayyalaraju Ramabhadrudu wrote the Ramabhyudayamu.
Pingali Surana wrote the Kalapurnodayamu and the Raghava Pandaviyamu.
Ramarajabhushanudu (Bhattumurthy) wrote the Vasucharitramu.
Tenali Ramakrishna wrote the Panduranga Mahatmyamu.
Saluva Timmarusu, called 'Appaji', was Krishnadevaraya's prime minister (Mahapradhana).
Achyuta Deva Raya (1529–1542) succeeded Krishnadevaraya; the Tiruvengalanatha (Achyutaraya) temple at Hampi was built in his reign.
Fernao Nunes, a Portuguese horse-trader, wrote his chronicle in Achyuta Raya's time (c.1535).
The Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi (AP), with its hanging pillar, was built by the brothers Virupanna and Viranna in Achyuta Raya's reign.
Sadasiva Raya (1542–1570) was a puppet; real power lay with Aliya Rama Raya, Krishnadevaraya's son-in-law.
The Talikota coalition was led by Ali Adil Shah I of Bijapur.
At Talikota Rama Raya was captured and beheaded on the orders of Hussain Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar.
Ibrahim Qutb Shah of Golconda joined the Talikota coalition.
Berar was the only Deccan Sultanate that did not join the Talikota coalition.
The Battle of Talikota is also called the Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi, after two villages on the Krishna.
The Battle of Talikota was fought on 23 January 1565.
After Talikota, Tirumala Deva Raya founded the Aravidu dynasty and moved the capital to Penukonda.
Venkata II (1586–1614) shifted the capital to Chandragiri.
In 1639, under Venkata III, the local nayaka Damarla Venkatadri granted the site of Madras to the English (Francis Day).
Sriranga III (1642–1646) was the last Vijayanagara ruler.
As the empire declined, the nayakas of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee and the Wodeyars of Mysore became independent.
Robert Sewell's 'A Forgotten Empire' (1900) made Vijayanagara known and translated Paes and Nunes.
Under the nayankara system the king assigned land to military chiefs (nayakas) who kept troops for him.
The military chiefs were called amaranayakas and the land they held was called amaram.
Amaranayakas paid an annual tribute to the king and supplied a fixed force of horses and elephants.
Crown land administered directly by the state was called bhandaravada.
Tax-free land grants were called manya — brahmadeya to Brahmins, devadana to temples and mathapura to mathas.
The ayagars were twelve hereditary village functionaries paid with tax-free land instead of salary.
The Karanam (accountant), Reddi or Gauda (headman) and Talari (watchman) were among the ayagars.
The standard gold coin was the varaha, called 'pagoda' by Europeans and 'hun' in Persian.
The pratapa was a gold coin worth half a varaha.
Smaller coins were the fanam (gold), tar (silver) and jital (copper).
Vijayanagara imported war-horses from Arabia and Persia through the Portuguese at Goa.
The Portuguese general Albuquerque took Goa from Bijapur in 1510 and sought Krishnadevaraya's friendship.
William Methwold, an English merchant (c.1630), described the decline after Talikota.
Foreign visitors such as Nicolo de Conti and Nunes describe sati among the Vijayanagara elite.
The Group of Monuments at Hampi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
The Virupaksha temple at Hampi is dedicated to Shiva as Pampapati; Krishnadevaraya added a hall and gopuram in 1510.
The stone chariot of the Vittala temple is a shrine to Garuda.
The huge entrance towers built by Vijayanagara rulers are called raya gopurams.
Pillared halls (kalyana mandapas) for the deity's marriage were a typical Vijayanagara addition.
The Lotus Mahal in the Zenana enclosure blends Indo-Islamic arches with Hindu forms.
The Elephant Stables at Hampi have eleven domed chambers.
The Hazara Rama temple, the royal chapel of Hampi with Ramayana friezes, dates from the early 15th century (Deva Raya I).
The Mahanavami Dibba (House of Victory) was the platform from which the king watched the Mahanavami festival.
One explanation derives the name 'Bahmani' from the Persian hero Bahman, whom the founder claimed as ancestor; Ferishta tells the Brahmin-Gangu legend.
Hasan Gangu renamed his capital Gulbarga as Ahsanabad.
Muhammad Shah I (1358–1375) fought Bukka I and Kapaya Nayaka; Kapaya ceded Golconda and the Turquoise Throne.
Muhammad Shah II (1378–1397) was a peaceful ruler who built mosques, madrasas and hospitals.
Firoz Shah Bahmani (1397–1422) built the city of Firozabad on the Bhima river.
Firoz Shah defeated the Gond Raja Narsing Rai of Kherla.
After his defeat at Pangal (1420) Firoz Shah abdicated in favour of his brother Ahmad Shah.
Ahmad Shah Wali annexed Warangal to the Bahmani kingdom (c.1425).
Gesu Daraz (Khwaja Bande Nawaz), a Chishti saint, is buried at Gulbarga.
Humayun Shah (1458–1461) was called 'Zalim' (the Cruel).
Muhammad Shah III became sultan at the age of nine (1463), with Mahmud Gawan as regent.
Afanasy (Athanasius) Nikitin, a Russian merchant from Tver, visited the Bahmani kingdom c.1469–1472.
After 1482 real power passed to the minister Qasim Barid, father of the Barid Shahi line.
Kalimullah Shah was the last Bahmani sultan (fled in 1527).
Mahmud Gawan came from Gilan in Persia.
Mahmud Gawan held the title 'Khwaja-i-Jahan' as chief minister.
Mahmud Gawan split the four large tarafs into eight to curb the provincial governors.
He let each tarafdar keep only one fort, placing the others under commanders sent from the centre.
He had land measured to fix the revenue demand.
Mahmud Gawan conquered Goa and Dabhol on the west coast.
The Bidar madrasa of Mahmud Gawan was built in 1472 and housed about 1,000 students.
Mahmud Gawan was executed (1481) on the strength of a forged letter planted by rival Deccani nobles.
Ferishta wrote the Tarikh-i-Ferishta (Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi) at Bijapur under Ibrahim Adil Shah II.
The Burhan-i-Maasir of Sayyid Ali Tabatabai is the chronicle of the Bahmanis and Nizam Shahis.
Manazir-ul-Insha of Mahmud Gawan is a Persian manual on the art of letter-writing.
Yusuf Adil Shah founded the Adil Shahi kingdom of Bijapur in 1489.
Malik Ahmad (Nizam-ul-Mulk Bahri) founded the Nizam Shahi kingdom of Ahmadnagar in 1490.
Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk founded the Imad Shahi kingdom of Berar (1490), with its capital at Ellichpur (Achalpur).
Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk founded the Qutb Shahi kingdom of Golconda in 1518.
The Barid Shahi kingdom of Bidar became independent under Amir Ali Barid (1528), son of Qasim Barid.
By about 1526 the Bahmani kingdom had broken up into the five Deccan Sultanates.
Berar, the shortest-lived Sultanate, was annexed by Ahmadnagar in 1574.
Bidar was annexed by Bijapur in 1619.
Ahmadnagar was finally annexed by Shah Jahan (1633–36).
Aurangzeb annexed Bijapur in 1686.
Aurangzeb annexed Golconda in 1687.
Chand Bibi defended Ahmadnagar against Akbar's Mughal army (1595–1600).
Malik Ambar, an Abyssinian (Habshi) minister of Ahmadnagar, fought the Mughals with guerrilla tactics and reformed land revenue.
Ibrahim Adil Shah I (1534–1558) replaced Persian with Hindvi (Dakhini) as the official language of Bijapur.
Ibrahim Adil Shah II (1580–1627) was called 'Jagadguru' and wrote the Kitab-i-Nauras in Dakhini.
Gol Gumbaz (completed 1656) at Bijapur, the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah, is famous for its whispering gallery.
Ibrahim Rauza at Bijapur is the tomb of Ibrahim Adil Shah II.
Bara Kaman at Bijapur is the unfinished tomb of Ali Adil Shah II.
The Jama Masjid at Gulbarga (1367) is unusual because its whole courtyard is roofed over with domes.
Haft Gumbaz (seven domes) at Gulbarga holds early Bahmani royal tombs.
The Rangeen Mahal and the Solah Khamba mosque are at Bidar.
Bidriware — silver inlay on a blackened zinc alloy — takes its name from Bidar.
